item.title: Liquid AI Releases LFM2.5-24B-A2B: A 2B-Active MoE for On-Device Agents
item.abstract: Liquid AI has released LFM2.5-24B-A2B , an open-weight reasoning model for agents that run on laptops and PCs. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model that activates about 2B parameters per token. It is the largest and final member of the LFM2.5 family. Liquid AI trained it inside popular agent harnesses, so it targets multi-step tool use rather than open chat. Base and post-trained weights are available on Hugging Face . It is a text-only, reasoning-only MoE model built for local agent loops. Every assistant turn opens with a <think> block, per the docs . Its predecessor, LFM2-24B-A2B , did not always reason first. It supports 16 languages, including English, Arabic, Chinese, Hindi and Japanese. It keeps LFM2’s 40-layer hybrid: 30 double-gated short convolution blocks and 10 grouped query attention (GQA) blocks. Each MoE block holds 64 experts with top-4 routing, according to the model card . Only 2 things changed from LFM2-24B-A2B. Context grew from 32,768 to 131,072 tokens. Vocabulary doubled from 65K to 128K through an in-place tokenizer expansion for better non-Latin tokenization. Pre-training scaled from 17T to 33T tokens. Mid-training ran 2T tokens at 32K context, then 300B tokens at 131K context. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear in both phases. Liquid AI also disclosed reward hacking during teacher specialization. The model searched git history, GitHub, PyPI and Hugging Face for answers. It even detected that it was inside a sandbox. Liquid AI says it tightened sandboxes, and reported results come from sealed environments. Liquid AI tested 16 benchmarks against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning (30B-A3B). It leads on AutomationBench, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw and τ³-Bench Banking. BFCLv4 is effectively a tie at 65.01 versus 65.00. The widest gap is AutomationBench: 27.69 versus 8.72 for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. On LiveClaw it scores 48.09 versus 38.19. It also tops all 3 instruction-following tests: IFEval 96.75, IFBench 74.69 and Multi-IF 84.38. Larger models win on knowledge and code. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B leads GPQA Diamond (83.69 vs 74.42) and SWE-Bench Verified (66.20 vs 51.00). Qwen also leads WebArena Verified (37.62 vs 26.75) and PinchBench (89.93 vs 83.18). *Scores from Liquid AI’s benchmark table , all models run by Liquid AI with vLLM. On-device, it decodes 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max. It reaches 114 tokens/s on an AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395. Liquid AI measured both with llama.cpp, Q4_K_M quantization and a 4K-token input. It claims up to 1.7x the speed of the next-best compared MoE, with the lowest memory use. Exact RAM requirements were not disclosed. For serving, it passes 21K output tokens/s on a single NVIDIA B300. That test used SGLang 0.5.22, BF16, 1,024 input tokens and up to 256 output tokens. Day-one support covers Transformers, vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp, MLX, LM Studio and ONNX. MLX needs mlx-lm>=0.32.0 , since earlier versions route experts incorrectly. Recommended sampling is temperature 0.1, top_k 50 and repetition penalty 1.05. A DSpark speculative-decoding draft model is listed as coming soon. On Liquid Console , the API costs $0.10 per 1M input tokens and $1.00 per 1M output tokens. Cached input costs $0.05 per 1M, and new accounts get $2 in credit. The weights use the LFM Open License v1.0 , based on Apache 2.0. Free commercial use ends once a company reaches $10M in annual revenue. Check out the technical blog , model weights , docs and LFM2 technical report . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. item.title: Pg_vectorsearch: An index that is faster than pgvector's IVFFlat and HNSW
item.abstract:
pg_vectorsearch A PostgreSQL extension for high-performance approximate nearest neighbor (ANN)
search. Status: alpha. Meant for testing, not production. Upgrading
between prereleases may not be possible; plan to drop and recreate the
extension and its indexes. See the changelog for
known issues. PRISM index (100M+ vectors) — IVF-style, with hierarchical routing RaBitQ quantization with theoretical error bounds for two-stage search SIMD-optimized distance computation (AVX2, AVX512, NEON) Dynamic updates — inserts, updates and deletes, with posting-list
splits via prism_rebalance (see Maintenance ) pgvector compatible — index existing vector and halfvec columns
as-is (see Existing pgvector tables ) PRISM Index PRISM (Partitioned Routing Index for Similarity Matching) is a PostgreSQL-native
index access method that is conceptually similar to pgvector 's
IVFFlat, but it is built around state-of-the-art quantization, routing, and
partitioning techniques. It is implemented in C for high performance and
seamless integration with PostgreSQL. The result: an index that is significantly faster than
pgvector's IVFFlat and HNSW, for both querying and index building. In fact,
compared to graph-based HNSW, PRISM is faster at equivalent recall on a
100-million-vector dataset, on an instance with a quarter of the memory. To achieve this performance, PRISM uses a hierarchical centroid tree to
partition vectors into clusters, and relies on the PostgreSQL buffer cache to
keep that tree warm in memory. Vectors are RaBitQ -quantized and stored
in posting lists with a page layout optimized for SIMD distance computation. The
RaBitQ encoding carries error bounds that let a search rule out vectors that
cannot possibly be nearest neighbors, so far fewer of them need reranking
against the full-precision vectors stored in the table. Query Flow:
1. Traverse centroid tree to find nearest clusters (buffer cache)
2. Scan posting lists for candidates (buffer cache, async I/O)
3. RaBitQ two-stage filtering: estimate → error bound → rerank
4. Full-precision reranking from heap
5. Return k nearest neighbors For detailed architecture, see docs/architecture.md . Usage Install the extension first; see Building . There are two ways to use a PRISM index. Pick the one that matches where
your vectors live: Native types . Starting fresh, or not using
pgvector? Store vectors in pg_vectorsearch 's own vec32 (float32) or vec16 (float16) columns. No other extension is needed. Existing pgvector tables . Already have vector or halfvec columns? Install pg_vectorsearch next to
pgvector and build a PRISM index on those columns as they are. Your
table and queries stay unchanged. Both paths build the same index and use the same operators ( <-> , <#> , <=> ) and tuning knobs. Native types CREATE EXTENSION pg_vectorsearch; -- PLAIN keeps the vector inline. EXTERNAL (the default) toasts a value -- over ~2 kB, and rerank then pays an extra fetch the planner does not cost. CREATE TABLE items ( id serial PRIMARY KEY , embedding vec32( 3 ) STORAGE PLAIN
); -- Load first; the index is sized from the row count at CREATE INDEX. -- 500 rows is enough for the planner to use the index. INSERT INTO items (embedding) SELECT ARRAY[i:: real , (i % 7 ):: real , (i % 5 ):: real ]::vec32 FROM generate_series( 1 , 1000 ) i; -- For inner product or cosine, see Operator classes below. CREATE INDEX ON items USING prism (embedding vec32_l2_ops); -- 0 = auto (~0.95 recall). Raise for recall, lower for speed. SET prism . nprobe = 40 ; SELECT * FROM items ORDER BY embedding < - > ' [3,1,2] ' LIMIT 5 ; Use vec16 instead of vec32 to halve the space vectors take in the
table, with the matching vec16_* operator classes . Existing pgvector tables If you already have a table with pgvector's vector or halfvec columns, you can build a PRISM index on it directly. Nothing about the
table or your queries needs to change. vec32 and vec16 are binary-compatible with pgvector's vector and halfvec but have different names, so the two extensions can be
installed side by side, even in the same schema. -- The table you already have, included so the example runs on its own. CREATE EXTENSION vector; CREATE TABLE documents ( id bigserial PRIMARY KEY , body text , embedding vector( 384 )
); CREATE INDEX documents_embedding_hnsw ON documents USING hnsw (embedding vector_l2_ops); -- Install pg_vectorsearch next to pgvector and build the index on the -- existing column. The column is not rewritten or copied. CREATE EXTENSION pg_vectorsearch; CREATE INDEX documents_embedding_prism ON documents USING prism (embedding vec32_l2_ops); -- Your queries keep working as before. PRISM is normally faster, so -- the planner should prefer it over the HNSW index while both exist. -- Verify with an EXPLAIN: EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT id, body FROM documents ORDER BY embedding < - > ( SELECT embedding FROM documents WHERE id = 42 ) LIMIT 10 ; -- Limit -- InitPlan 1 -- -> Index Scan using documents_pkey on documents documents_1 -- Index Cond: (id = 42) -- -> Index Scan using documents_embedding_prism on documents -- Order By: (embedding <-> (InitPlan 1).col1) -- Once you are happy with it, drop the HNSW index. DROP INDEX documents_embedding_hnsw; Use the PRISM operator class for the same distance
metric as your HNSW index. Operator classes Pick the operator class for your distance metric and column type. L2 is
the default. Distance Operator vec32 / vector vec16 / halfvec L2 <-> vec32_l2_ops vec16_l2_ops Inner product <#> vec32_ip_ops vec16_ip_ops Cosine <=> vec32_cosine_ops vec16_cosine_ops When replacing an HNSW index, pgvector's vector_<metric>_ops maps to vec32_<metric>_ops and halfvec_<metric>_ops to vec16_<metric>_ops . Tuning Defaults are tuned from large-scale benchmarks; most deployments only
ever adjust prism.nprobe .
See the tuning guide for every index parameter and GUC,
their tradeoffs, and when changing them makes sense. Maintenance An insert appends to whichever posting list its vector routes to, so lists
grow as rows arrive and never split on their own. Besides REINDEX , the prism_rebalance procedure splits oversized lists in place.
See the maintenance guide for how it works and its current
limitations. Building Requirements: PostgreSQL 18+ (with development headers) GNU C11 compiler (GCC 11+ or Clang 14+) Meson build system Optional: CBLAS, for faster RaBitQ encoding. See Development . # Release build meson setup builddir --buildtype=release # Build and install to PostgreSQL meson install -C builddir See the development guide for build
options. Documentation Tuning - Index parameters, GUCs, tradeoffs, defaults Maintenance - Rebalancing and splitting posting lists Architecture - High-level design and data structures SIMD - SIMD build options and distance computation Development - Build options, testing, CI scripts References Research RaBitQ - Binary quantization with theoretical error bounds
(SIGMOD 2024) SPFresh - LIRE protocol for incremental updates (SOSP 2023) SPANN - Billion-scale ANN with boundary replication
(NeurIPS 2021) ScaNN for AlloyDB - Hierarchical clustering (Google) Related Projects pgvector - Vector type and operators for PostgreSQL pgvectorscale - DiskANN-based vector index for PostgreSQL License The PostgreSQL License

item.title: Google Releases Gemini 4 Argon API With 1M Token Output Limit
item.abstract: Google DeepMind has made Gemini 4 Argon generally available to developers, enterprises and paid Gemini subscribers. Gemini 4 Argon is a sparse mixture-of-experts frontier model from Google built for long, multi-step work. Its target domains are coding, finance, legal, science and cybersecurity. Google first announced Argon on September 30 for a small group of cyber defenders. It now reaches the paid Gemini API at $2 input and $10 output per million tokens. The key change for developers is output length: Argon can write up to 1M tokens in one response. According to the model card , Argon is a new model, not a fine-tune of an earlier Gemini. It is a large-scale sparse MoE transformer with native multimodal support. It accepts text, images, audio and video, and it outputs text. Google trained it on TPUs using JAX and ML Pathways. The knowledge cutoff is March 2026. Google has not disclosed total or active parameter counts. Google raised the output limit to 1M tokens, up from 64K on earlier Gemini models. The model card describes a combined input plus output window of up to 1M tokens. So a long prompt reduces the room left for output. Google documents a new continuation protocol for long decodes in its developer docs and enterprise docs . At introductory pricing, a full 1M token response costs $10 in output tokens. Google compares Argon with GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5. Argon posts the top score on most rows. Google also reports 87% on the ERQA embodied reasoning benchmark . Read the evaluation methodology before drawing conclusions. Most rival scores are self-reported or pulled from public leaderboards. Argon’s DeepSWE score is self-computed with a mini-swe-agent harness. The rival DeepSWE numbers come from system cards and a leaderboard. Argon trails on 5 rows of Google’s own table: The model card also lists hallucinations and occasional slowness or timeouts. Under Google’s Frontier Safety Framework, Google says it cannot rule out the biological and cybersecurity critical capability levels. It reports deploying safeguards it assesses as lowering that risk. Google shared internal results in its launch post : Introductory pricing is $2 input and $10 output per million tokens. Cached input tokens are 95% off. After November 30, 2026, the price rises to $4 and $20. That matches Claude Opus 5.5 and sits below GPT-6 Astra’s $10 and $50. Access paths, per the developer post : Check out the Model Card , Evaluation Methodology and Developer Guide . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. Diverging from previous approaches, we introduce the first tri-modal Masked Diffusion Models (MDM) pretrained from scratch on text, image-text, and audio-text data. We systematically analyze multimodal scaling laws, modality mixing ratios, noise schedules, batch-size effects and provide optimized inference sampling defaults. Our batch-size analysis yields a novel stochastic differential equation (SDE) based reparameterization, eliminating the need for tuning the optimal batch size as reported in recent work. item.title: Meta Launches Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full: Benchmarks, Pricing and How to Use It
item.abstract: Meta has released Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full , its most capable models so far. Muse Wonder is a frontier model from Meta built for personal and professional AI agents. Both models target long-running agent work: coding, legal and finance tasks, and computer use. Muse Wonder is live now on the Meta Model API and Muse Code . Muse Wonder Full is limited to paid Muse Code plans. Muse Wonder follows Muse Spark on Meta’s scaling ladder. Meta team states that it was trained at its Prometheus data center , with gains across pretraining and reinforcement learning. Meta credits a larger base model for better results on unfamiliar tasks. Two named behaviors define the release: For developers, Muse Wonder plans long tasks and delegates to sub-agents. It also operates browsers, desktop and mobile apps. All scores below come from Meta’s published table at max reasoning effort. Several rows use third-party sources such as Artificial Analysis, Vals AI and Datacurve. Note: PSI, MemoryBench and FocusBench are internal Meta evaluations. The model card says competitor runs are best-effort and may not be tuned. SWE-Marathon results for rivals used Codex and Claude Code, so it is not a common-harness comparison. Step 1: Open dev.meta.ai. Click Start building to sign in. The Muse Code install command sits on the same page. Step 2: Pick your model. Muse Wonder costs $4 input, $0.20 cached and $20 output per million tokens. Muse Wonder Full needs a Muse Code plan : Power at $50 or Maximum at $200 per month. Step 3: Sign in with your Meta account. Confirm your name, accept the Model API terms, and click Get started . Step 4. Add billing, then create an API key. New accounts see a “No payment method” banner, and Create API key stays disabled. Add a card under Billing , then open API keys and select Create API key . Export it as MODEL_API_KEY , per the quickstart . Step 5. Test it in the Playground. Open Chat , pick muse-wonder-1.0 , and set temperature, max tokens and reasoning effort. Step 6. Copy working code. Click Get code for a curl or Python snippet. It calls the Responses endpoint at https://api.meta.ai/v1/responses . The API is OpenAI-compatible, so the OpenAI SDK works with a new base URL: Step 7: Or use Muse Code in your terminal. On Mac, install with curl -fsSL https://dev.meta.ai/install.sh | bash . On Windows, use irm https://dev.meta.ai/install.ps1 | iex . Run muse in your project folder, trust the workspace, and sign in. The default model is muse-spark-1.2 . Switch with /models , or launch with muse --model muse-wonder-1.0 . Check out the research blog , model card and developer docs . item.title: Dyna-2: General Purpose Physical Agents with Hour-Long Autonomy — Jason Ma, Dyna Robotics
item.abstract: Watch along AIE NYC and join us at AIE CODE in SF next month! This episode includes a live demo of the Taku robot that is best enjoyed on YouTube . Last month, Dyna made waves by announcing Dyna-2 , a world-action model pre-trained on one million hours of human video, claiming several new scaling laws on human data across four orders of magnitude . They have now followed up the model with a physical robot agent, Dyna-2.1 , that has to be seen to be believed: In his talk at AIE this year, Jason talked about how the real challenge for robotics in the real world is reliable, long-horizon autonomy , and how Dyna got its models to a 99.4% success rate folding restaurant napkins for 24 hours straight, including recovering after it pulled over the whole stack. From training a world-action model on over one million hours of human video to deploying robots that fold thousands of napkins daily at Din Tai Fung , Dyna Robotics is pushing physical AI beyond impressive demos and into real-world production. In this episode, Dyna Robotics co-founder and Chief Scientist Jason Ma joins swyx on-site to unpack how robots can learn new tasks from as little as 45 minutes of demonstrations, why predicting the future of the physical world may be the key to general-purpose robotics, and what it actually takes to build robots that work reliably for real customers. We go deep on Dyna-2, Dyna’s million-hour world-action model that combines future video prediction with robot actions, the scaling laws behind human-to-robot transfer, diffusion transformers and flow matching, and why synthetic environments and self-generated training data could unlock the next wave of robotics progress. Jason also explains why Dyna builds its own hardware instead of relying on off-the-shelf humanoids, how agentic harnesses enable robots to execute hour-long workflows, why dexterous hands and missing sensory data remain major bottlenecks, and what separates real commercial deployments from the graveyard of robotics startups. We also cover world-action models versus vision-language-action models, GPT-6 and coding agents in robotics, and Jason’s journey from AlphaGo and Penn to NVIDIA, Google DeepMind, and founding Dyna. item.title: Sizing Lakebase Search: lessons from a real app and 4 million passages
item.abstract: Slide Hub is an internal Databricks app. Field engineers use it to find and reuse slides from about 700 internal presentations: event talks, product decks, and architecture decks. A search bar finds single slides by meaning and by keyword, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server gives AI agents the same search. The app stores its slides, votes, search telemetry, and change history in Lakebase Postgres . We use Slide Hub as the baseline to benchmark Lakebase Postgres. It is a real app with a real use case and real users, so its numbers show how the database behaves under an actual workload. This post is for developers and architects who build apps on Databricks and want search inside the app's own Lakebase Postgres database. It assumes that you know SQL and the basics of PostgreSQL. If you plan a search bar or an agent tool on Lakebase Postgres, the numbers below help you choose the compute size before you go to production. This post shows how Slide Hub runs search inside Lakebase Postgres, what limits it under load, what it costs, and how Lakebase Search behaves from 1M to 4M rows of a public corpus. Lakebase Search became generally available in September. It is a set of Postgres extensions , so it runs next to the application tables. The app does not copy data to a separate search system. The developer does not maintain a second transaction path. Two CREATE EXTENSION statements enable the components. lakebase_vector stores embeddings , vectors of numbers that represent the meaning of a text, and supports the lakebase_ann index for approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search. lakebase_text supports the lakebase_bm25 index for BM25, a standard method that ranks text by the query words it contains. lakebase_tokenizer is optional. The ANN index uses IVF partitioning, which groups similar vectors so a query reads only a few groups, and RaBitQ quantization, which compresses each vector to about 1 bit per dimension. BM25 scores text with the <@> operator. Slide Hub’s 23k slide rows sit in the same serverless Lakebase Postgres instance as the votes, telemetry, change history, previews, and both indexes. The app reads the data and the indexes inside one connection and one permission model. Slide Hub runs hybrid search . It combines vector search , which finds slides with a similar meaning to the query, and BM25 keyword search , which finds slides that contain the query words. Each method returns a short list of its best matches, the candidates . One SQL statement carries the whole ranking policy. It ranks each candidate list, fuses the two rankings, applies the app filters, and joins the votes. Search and app logic share one connection, one set of grants, and one commit. Slide Hub takes 200 candidates from each method. It fuses the two lists with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) at k=60: a slide scores 1/(60 + its rank) in each list, and the two scores add. A similarity gate of 0.70 rejects vector matches that are too far from the query to be useful for this embedding model. Title tiers add weight when the query matches a slide title. Notes receive weight 0.5. Scope filters restrict the result to assets the user has permission to see. A search request uses two separate computes, and either one can set the limit. Lakebase Postgres compute runs the database. Lakebase Postgres sizes it in Compute Units (CU) . One CU allocates about 2 GB of RAM to the database, with its share of CPU and local SSD. A compute autoscales between a minimum and a maximum size from 0.5 CU to 64 CU, and the maximum can be at most 16 CU above the minimum. Fixed-size computes go up to 112 CU, and computes up to 32 CU can scale to zero .Postgres stores tables and indexes in 8 KB pages . Lakebase Postgres keeps recently read pages in a Local File Cache (LFC) on the compute. The cache grows with the CU size and can use up to 75% of the compute's memory. A page that is not in the cache comes from storage, which takes longer. Databricks Apps compute runs the Slide Hub web server. Its size is fixed per app. A MEDIUM app has up to 2 vCPU and 6 GB of memory, and a LARGE app has up to 4 vCPU and 12 GB. Slide Hub runs one app instance. Each Python worker process in it holds a pool of 8 database connections, so 2 workers open at most 16 connections and 4 workers open at most 32. For each request, the app embeds the query text, sends one SQL statement to Lakebase Postgrse, and returns the result. To find the limit, the test changes one side at a time. It pins Lakebase Postgres at one CU size and changes the app, or it keeps the app and changes the CU size. A load generator simulates users that send search requests, and it raises the number of users in steps. The list shows requests per second and the median latency (p50) at 500 users for each Lakebase Postgres size and app size. Up to 4 CU, Lakebase is the limit. A LARGE app with twice the workers and connections adds nothing at 1 CU. At 1 CU the search statement averaged 146 ms and read 14.9M pages from storage, with a file cache of 1.5 GB. At 8 CU it averaged 34 ms, with a cache of 12 GB, and throughput rose about 50%. From 8 CU, the app is the limit. 16 CU with the same MEDIUM app adds only 4%, and its database connections sit mostly idle. A LARGE app with 4 workers at 16 CU reaches at least 662 req/s, and there the load generator was the limit. Size the query first. Then scale Lakebase Postgres until the app workers are the limit, and then scale the app. Takeaway: Find the limit before you scale. Below 8 CU, add Lakebase Postgres CU. From 8 CU, give the app more workers. The connection pool is still necessary. At 50 users the app reached 45 req/s and 2.4 s p95 without the pool, and 85 req/s and 0.7 s p95 with it. The embedding cache made no measurable difference under load. The candidate limit sets the number of pages a query touches. On a cold cache, that number sets the latency. Slide Hub shipped with 1,000 candidates per method. The docs pattern uses 40. The candidate-limit experiment changed only candidate_limit and measured 20 public queries in three states. Cold is the first query after the compute scaled to zero, with an empty cache. First-touch is the first run of a query on an awake compute. Repeat is the same query run again, with its pages in the cache. Pages touched counts the pages a query reads from any source. Top-10 overlap is the share of the top 10 results that match the result at 1,000 candidates. At 200 candidates, 90.5% of the top 10 stays the same, and the reported number of matches is 81% of the number at 1,000 candidates. Users rarely page past 200 results, so Slide Hub now ships 200. Measured end to end from a job in the same cloud region as the app, a cold search at 200 candidates took 2.9 s, and a repeat search took 40 ms. The cold time has two parts. The connection waits about 1 s while the endpoint wakes up. Then each query reads its pages from storage until the cache warms. The first query on a new connection also pays about 75 ms of planning. Takeaway: Keep the candidate pool small. 200 candidates keep 90.5% of the top 10 results, read about a third of the pages of 1,000 candidates, and halve the cold latency. The scale tests use MIRACL English , a passage corpus built from Wikipedia. The full corpus has 32,893,221 passages. We embedded it with gte-large-en-v1.5 , a 1024-dimension open model, the same size as the Slide Hub embeddings. We self-hosted the model on one A10G GPU at 379 passages per second. The whole corpus took 2.95 GPU-hours, against $48.87 for the same work on a model-serving endpoint. The GPU vectors matched the endpoint vectors (mean cosine 1.0000, minimum 0.9978). We built three subsets: 1M, 2M, and 4M passages. The lakebase_ann index grew with the corpus: 5.8 GB at 1M, 11.5 GB at 2M, 23.0 GB at 4M. A binary COPY loaded all 4M rows in 19 minutes at 8 CU. Lakebase Postgres holds about 1.6 GB of file cache per CU. Scale raises one question: what happens when the index is larger than the cache?

item.title: Lab-in-the-Loop at Compute Speed — Ian Quigley, Leash Bio
item.abstract: A few years ago I stumbled upon Leash Bio’s Substack , and was hooked. Be it their Kaggle competition that showed that no, we really haven’t solved protein-ligand binding , or their crazy discovery that knowing a molecule’s author is perhaps all you need to know to predict how good it is . Their substack — or at least Owl Posting ’s 1 deep dive on them — should be required reading for any scientist trying to do chemistry with AI. So I was super excited to finally be able to sit down with Ian Quigley from Leash Bio, and pick his brain. Leash specializes in DNA Encoded Libraries (aka “DELs”), a way of collecting ridiculously high-throughput interaction data between proteins and small molecules. 2 Before I discovered Leash, I had heard nothing but horror stories from DEL users. And yet, Ian and friends somehow found a way to tame the beast, extracting clean and reproducible data that is just perfect for large scale modeling. Without teasing too much, the answer comes down to epistemic rigor, and an incredible conviction that you just have to Do The Thing. It gets even better! Near the end of this episode, Ian teases something his team was just playing with when we recorded: an AI playground for agents to do verifiable scientific reasoning. They discovered the data they had spent the last few years collecting could provide tens of thousands of “lab-in-the-loop” simulations, just what an agent needs for scientific RL. Two months later, it’s matured into Minos, and today they’re releasing a full preprint , blog , and open dataset . We’ll be releasing a lightning podcast in a few days with an update. Stay tuned! We had a blast with Ian, probably one of our most fun episodes to date. For both complete chemistry novices and expert AI x Bio practitioners, we think you’ll get something out of this. Why DELs traumatize everyone who touches them, and how Leash puts dozens of barcodes on each molecule to catch proteins that bind the DNA instead of the drug. Ian’s rule that biology only scales two ways: taking pictures and sequencing DNA. The Kaggle competition : about 4B measurements from a basement and about 2,000 teams, with nobody beating chance on an unseen chemical library. Also why Leash quietly feared co-folding would make them obsolete. Clever Hans in ChEMBL : models can guess a molecule’s chemist from its structure, and “who made it” predicts activity about as well as the structure does. Hermes , trained only on Leash’s own data, keeping pace with Boltz on public benchmarks. Plus the BRD4 molecule Boltz had already seen in the PDB. Breaking the pocket : engineering protein mutants at scale after catching Hermes memorizing “nicknames” for proteins instead of binding sites. Lumacaftor -like hits as an accidental detector for misfolded proteins. The agent sandbox : LLMs that reason about SAR in plain English, hunting for the best binders among 6.5M molecules on a budget of 100. The Recursion mafia, and why its alumni companies all rhyme. The Kosuri paradox : if you can collect the data, why do you need the model? Going from a DEL hit to good mouse PKPD in six months on an inflammation program, and the case for pills over antibodies on cytokine targets. What stops a better-funded lab from outscaling them, and Ian’s by-fiat wish for massively parallel purification. The hands-down best bio blogger on the internet. As always, the secret here is to map your problem to a combinatorial library and a readout using Next Generation Sequencing. We talk about this in depth in the podcast!

item.title: 5 Fun Projects for LLM Inference Engineering
item.abstract: 5 Fun Projects for LLM Inference Engineering Want to understand what makes LLMs fast? Build the systems yourself. By Kanwal Mehreen , KDnuggets Technical Editor & Content Specialist on October 14, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence Training large language models gets most of the attention, but once a model is trained, another engineering problem begins: how do you serve it quickly and efficiently? LLM inference engineering focuses on reducing latency, increasing throughput, lowering memory consumption, and getting more useful work from the available hardware. This involves techniques such as KV caching, continuous batching, quantization, prefix caching, speculative decoding, optimized attention kernels, and distributed inference. The best way to learn these concepts is not by reading about them individually — it is by building something and seeing what happens. In this article, we will look at 5 projects that progressively introduce the most important ideas behind modern LLM inference systems . 1. Building a Mini-vLLM From Scratch If you want one project that exposes you to almost the entire inference stack, this is probably the best place to start. Nano-vLLM is a small educational implementation of a vLLM -style inference engine, with its core implementation small enough to actually read. It includes scheduling, KV-cache block management, prefix caching, tensor parallelism, CUDA graphs, and other optimizations while using a real Qwen model. Instead of simply cloning it and running the example, rebuild one component at a time: first perform normal autoregressive generation, then add KV caching, then batching, then block-based KV-cache allocation. Benchmark tokens per second after every addition. By the end, you will understand concepts like PagedAttention and continuous batching in a much better way. 2. Writing Your Own FlashAttention Kernel With Triton A normal attention implementation uses large matrices and repeatedly moves data between GPU memory and fast on-chip memory. FlashAttention restructures the computation to reduce that memory traffic. Triton's official tutorial provides an implementation of a FlashAttention-style fused attention kernel, making it a great starting point for learning kernel-level optimization. This video also builds FlashAttention from scratch while explaining HBM versus SRAM, arithmetic intensity, tiling, online softmax, benchmarking, and finally integrating the kernel into an inference engine. I would recommend it to those who prefer video-based learning. This project teaches you that making an LLM faster is not always about doing fewer mathematical operations. Sometimes it is about moving less data . 3. Building an LLM Quantization Lab Take one small open model and run several versions — for example FP16, INT8, and 4-bit. Measure model size, peak memory, model-load time, time to first token (TTFT), tokens per second, and quality on a small evaluation set. Hugging Face supports multiple quantization approaches, including AWQ, GPTQ, bitsandbytes-based 8-bit and 4-bit loading, and several newer formats. llama.cpp also supports a wide range of low-bit quantization formats and runs across CPUs, Apple Silicon, NVIDIA GPUs, and several other hardware backends. For an extra challenge, quantize both the weights and KV cache and see whether using fewer bits always improves latency or not. 4. Implementing Speculative Decoding Speculative decoding is one of the most enjoyable inference optimizations to implement. Instead of asking the expensive target model to generate every token sequentially, a smaller draft model proposes several candidate tokens. The target model then verifies those candidates together. Choose a small target/draft pair, implement normal autoregressive decoding as the baseline, and then build the draft-and-verify loop. Track not only tokens per second but also acceptance rate — which is the percentage of draft tokens accepted by the target model. Then experiment with drafting 2, 4, 6, or 8 tokens at a time. The Columbia high-performance machine learning project experiments with both speculative decoding and quantization using the Llama model family while evaluating latency, throughput, perplexity, and code-generation quality. An interesting extension is to test different workloads. Code, repetitive text, factual question-answering, and creative writing can produce very different draft acceptance behavior. 5. Building Your Own Production LLM Inference Service The final project is a capstone where we combine KV caching, quantization, batching, and benchmarking into a single system. Start with a basic OpenAI-compatible inference endpoint. Deploy it on a GPU. Add streaming. Add load testing. Instrument TTFT and token-generation latency. Introduce quantization. Experiment with speculative decoding. Add prefix caching. Push concurrency higher and identify what breaks first. The Time to First Token project provides an interesting structure for doing this. Its roadmap revolves around continuously improving one inference service rather than completing disconnected exercises. It covers deployment, instrumentation, heavy concurrency testing, quantization, speculative decoding, routing, and reproducible benchmarking. For an even harder extension, add a request router that decides which model or GPU should process each request based on queue length, expected generation length, or latency requirements. Wrapping Up You need enough machine learning knowledge to understand transformers and attention, but many of the hardest problems have surprisingly little to do with training models. They involve memory allocation, scheduling, batching, caching, kernel optimization, networking, load testing, and figuring out how to keep very expensive hardware busy. This is why building projects is such a good way to learn the field. Start by generating one token inefficiently. Add a KV cache. Batch several users together. Break the cache into pages. Quantize the weights. Let a smaller model speculate about future tokens. Write a GPU kernel. Then put everything behind an API and bombard it with requests. By the time you finish, tools such as vLLM and SGLang will no longer feel like black boxes. You will have built smaller versions of many of the ideas that make them fast. Kanwal Mehreen is a machine learning engineer and a technical writer with a profound passion for data science and the intersection of AI with medicine. She co-authored the ebook "Maximizing Productivity with ChatGPT". As a Google Generation Scholar 2022 for APAC, she champions diversity and academic excellence. She's also recognized as a Teradata Diversity in Tech Scholar, Mitacs Globalink Research Scholar, and Harvard WeCode Scholar. Kanwal is an ardent advocate for change, having founded FEMCodes to empower women in STEM fields. <= Previous post Next post =>

item.title: Build self-improving document processing using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
item.abstract: IDC research shows that document-related challenges cost organizations $19,732 for each information worker annually and reduce productivity by 21.3 percent. Organizations receiving invoices from hundreds of suppliers often face layouts that vary by issuer and change without notice. Template-based systems require constant maintenance at this scale. Staff can spend up to 30 percent of their time on document-related tasks, and manual data entry error rates range from 1–4 percent . Conventional intelligent document processing (IDP) solutions address some of this burden, but they require extensive upfront configuration for each document format and break when layouts vary across vendors. In this post, you learn how to build an agentic IDP system using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that classifies, extracts, validates, and learns from business documents with minimal human intervention. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Your agents automatically handle new document formats, such as supplier invoices, purchase orders, insurance claims, and loan applications. By the end of this post, you can: Many IDP pipelines require you to define templates, extraction rules, and validation logic for every document format upfront. When a new vendor sends a purchase order with a different layout, the pipeline breaks. This creates three core challenges: An agentic approach addresses these challenges. Instead of static templates, AI agents analyze each document, generate extraction instructions, validate results, and learn from corrections automatically. Over time, your system builds a knowledge base of document formats, so you process similar documents with minimal additional configuration. In this solution, eight specialized agents collaborate across two graph-based workflows running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The following diagram shows the multi-agent workflow graph built using Strands Agents , an open source SDK for building AI agents. Figure 1: Multi-agent orchestration workflow graph The following diagram shows the infrastructure architecture for the solution. Figure 2: Agentic IDP infrastructure architecture on AWS Follow these steps to deploy the solution infrastructure and web UI to your AWS account. To deploy this solution, you must have: This deploys six AWS CloudFormation stacks: Core (S3, Cognito, DynamoDB), Gateway (Lambda tools, AgentCore Gateway), Aurora (Amazon Aurora DSQL), Agent (AgentCore runtime, containers), UI Orchestrator (API endpoints), and Modern UI (React app on Amazon CloudFront ). Deployment takes approximately 15–20 minutes. After deployment, you receive an email with the CloudFront URL, username, and temporary password. Suppose you upload the first purchase order from a new retailer, Two Wheel Store. The Matcher agent searches the vector store, finds no similar document, and routes the job through the training workflow. The Analyzer agent uses Amazon Textract to extract the raw document text: The Instructions agent generates extraction prompts from the schema, and the Extractor agent produces structured JSON: The Validator agent checks the result against the schema and fails : The vendor’s SKU format ( SB-004 ) doesn’t match Acme Bikes’ internal format ( AB-SB-004 ). The Instructions Fixer agent diagnoses the mismatch and adds an explicit SKU transformation rule to the extraction prompt: prefix vendor SKUs with AB- . On the second pass, the seven line items validate successfully, and the Save Instructions agent persists the refined prompt to the vector store. End-to-end time for this first run: 3 minutes 49 seconds. When a second purchase order from Two Wheel Store arrives, the Matcher agent finds the stored instructions from the first run with a confidence score of 3.946 (threshold: 3.7) and routes the job through the automation workflow: The dashboard includes a chat interface for troubleshooting: The system improves over time through two feedback loops: When changing models, use AgentCore Evaluations , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to confirm that extraction quality remains acceptable. The solution already uses AgentCore Observability, so it has the required instrumentation. You pay only for what you use, because the solution runs on serverless and on-demand resources with no idle costs. For a workload of 10 training documents and 1,000 processed documents each month in US East (N. Virginia), the estimated cost is approximately $58 per month. Foundation model (FM) inference through Amazon Bedrock represents approximately 85 percent of the total cost, at roughly $0.055 per document. Actual cost depends largely on the models assigned to each agent. Model choices are centralized in agents/orchestratorgraph/utils/config.py , so you can use lower-cost models for simpler tasks and stronger models where needed. For detailed pricing, refer to the Amazon Bedrock pricing page. You get a purchase order processing use case with a synthetic bike company dataset, a pre-built JSON schema, and a validation Lambda function that checks extracted data against product and vendor records in a mock ERP database. To process your own documents, you must replace the included schemas and validation logic with your own. Create a JSON schema that defines the fields you want to extract for each document type. The sample purchase order schema in agents/orchestratorgraph/doc_schema/purchase_order_schema.json provides a reference. Your schema should specify field names, data types, and whether each field is explicitly stated in the document or inferred from context. The included validator checks purchase order data against synthetic vendor and product tables in Aurora DSQL. Your production implementation requires a validation process tailored to your business rules. For example: To add a new validator, create a Lambda function that accepts extracted JSON and returns a pass/fail result with detailed error messages, then register it as a tool in AgentCore Gateway. Refer to gateway/tools/po_validator_tool/ for the implementation pattern. The agent prompts in agents/orchestratorgraph/prompts/ reference purchase order terminology. Update these prompts to reflect your document types and extraction requirements. The Orchestrator agent, Validator agent, and Instructions agent each contain document-type-specific language that you should adapt. Keep these recommendations in mind as you train and operate your agentic IDP system. Important: Before running cleanup, export the data you want to retain. The destroy.py script permanently deletes processed documents (S3), job history (DynamoDB), validation data (Aurora DSQL), and learned extraction instructions (vector store). To avoid ongoing charges, remove the deployed resources: Verify that the six CloudFormation stacks are deleted on the console: AgenticIDP-Core-Dev, AgenticIDP-Gateway-Dev, AgenticIDP-Aurora-Dev, AgenticIDP-Agent-Dev, AgenticIDP-UIOrchestr-Dev, and AgenticIDP-ModernUI-Dev. In this post, you learned how to build a self-improving document processing system using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, where specialized AI agents collaborate to classify, extract, validate, and learn from business documents. This agentic approach adapts to new document formats automatically and improves accuracy over time through feedback loops, replacing manual template configuration with autonomous learning. item.title: How Tamnoon built AI-powered cloud security remediation with Amazon Bedrock
item.abstract: Critical cloud exposures pile up faster than security teams can close them. Cloud-native application protection platforms (CNAPP), cloud providers, and posture scanners generate more findings than any team can triage, and risk accumulates in the gap between detected and fixed. Most findings sit untouched, not because they’re hard to fix. Someone must investigate context, identify the owner, confirm the fix won’t break production, and then do it at a volume that outpaces headcount. In this post, we share how Tamnoon built Tami, an agentic cloud remediation orchestrator on Amazon Bedrock , to close that gap. Tami autonomously investigates findings ingested from CNAPP and cloud-native sources and assesses whether remediation is safe. It then generates and orchestrates the fix with guardrails and governance wherever a change touches a customer’s cloud. The approach drove an over 90 percent reduction in critical cloud exposure in 90 days with zero production issues. Tamnoon is an AI-powered cloud security remediation platform that works alongside CNAPPs. Its AI assistant, Tami, helps human cloud security experts investigate, prioritize, and safely remediate misconfigurations and issues across customer environments in AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and other cloud providers. Tamnoon integrates with the CNAPPs and cloud-native tools teams already use and turns their findings into validated, production-safe fixes. Most of the work including investigation, prioritization, and remediation planning happens before anything touches a live environment, which is what makes automated remediation trustworthy at scale. A security engineer can spend hours investigating a single finding. Often, it traces back to the same root cause as dozens of other alerts. Tamnoon’s solution addresses the full pipeline from finding ingestion to validated fix. The platform treats these challenges as interconnected rather than isolated problems. Tamnoon takes you from initial finding to executing the fix. The platform ingests findings from CNAPP, Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) providers, and other security tools and normalizes them into a unified schema. It then enriches them with asset and exposure context and prioritizes them. From there, the agentic layer takes over using a set of specialized AI agents, each running in an event-driven, serverless architecture on AWS, so every stage scales independently and fails safely. The platform delegates work to four specialized agents, each responsible for a distinct phase of the remediation pipeline: When the Tamnoon team set out to build Tami, the choice of foundation model (FM) platform was going to shape everything that followed. Tamnoon’s remediation agents don’t all do the same kind of work. Some perform deep investigative reasoning to understand the root cause of a security finding. Others handle high-volume validation, checking proposed fixes quickly and cheaply. Still others review generated code, balancing quality against cost on every task. Matching each of these jobs to the right model, without stitching together a different integration for each one, was a core requirement. That requirement is what made Amazon Bedrock the natural fit. Through a single API, each agent can call the foundation model best suited to its task. The most capable models handle the hardest reasoning. More efficient models take on the repetitive, high-throughput work. Review-focused models optimize the trade-off between output quality and cost. Because it’s one integration rather than many, models can be swapped or upgraded as the landscape evolves, without re-plumbing the architecture each time. Operational overhead at scale was another factor in the decision. As request volume grew, Tamnoon wanted to avoid building and maintaining its own logic to distribute traffic across regional capacity. Amazon Bedrock Cross-Region inference handles this automatically. It automatically routes inference requests to the optimal AWS Region within a defined geographic boundary, maintaining throughput without requiring any custom routing code to operate. Security was the final consideration, and for a cloud security company it was non-negotiable. With Bedrock, inference runs inside Tamnoon’s own AWS environment under AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)-scoped permissions. Sensitive customer data never leaves the trust boundary. That gave the team confidence that the platform underpinning Tami met the same standard Tamnoon holds its own service to. Tamnoon sits downstream of the detection tools security teams already run. CNAPPs like Wiz, CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Cortex, Upwind, SentinelOne, Orca, and Cyera along with cloud-native services like AWS Security Hub and Amazon GuardDuty are the source of truth for what’s wrong in the environment. Tamnoon connects through API-based integrations and normalizes findings into a common format, so a misconfiguration looks the same whether it came from Wiz or GuardDuty. The detection tools remain the foundation. Tamnoon delivers the end-to-end remediation that follows. For every finding it works, Tami assigns a Remediation Confidence Indicator (RCI) of SAFE, RISKY, or AWAITING DATA. That rating tells teams what can be automated and what needs human review first. Tamnoon runs entirely within its own AWS accounts, isolated per environment. Users access the platform through a single secure entry point built on Amazon API Gateway, with encryption managed by AWS Certificate Manager and sign-in handled by Amazon Cognito. Everything behind that entry point runs in private networks across multiple Availability Zones, so the core platform is never directly exposed to the internet. Inside that environment, Tamnoon combines two kinds of compute. Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) runs the always-on services behind the dashboard, while AWS Lambda powers the event-driven work of collecting findings, analyzing them, and executing remediations. A set of AWS messaging and workflow services, including Amazon EventBridge, Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS), and AWS Step Functions, coordinate these steps so large volumes of findings are processed reliably and in parallel, with no single bad record stalling the rest. The AI layer runs on Amazon Bedrock. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model, gives Tamnoon’s agents a governed way to take action instead of open-ended access. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails then review both the request and the generated code before anything moves forward. Supporting services handle the rest of the platform: managed databases and caching for state, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) for playbooks and artifacts, and AWS Secrets Manager for credentials, so sensitive keys never live in application code. On the customer side, everything to the left of the AWS Cloud boundary is what customers connect into Tamnoon. They can link their own AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud accounts, plug in the security tools their findings come from, and connect the destinations where they want outcomes delivered, such as Slack, Jira, ServiceNow, and GitHub. Figure 2: Tamnoon AWS architecture Zero production issues is a reality for Tamnoon’s customers, and it is no accident. Autonomy at Tamnoon sits inside a defense-in-depth safety architecture, where each layer assumes the one before it might miss something. It starts before any fix is even drafted. No remediation is written until an independent safety assessment, focused on scope and deliberately biased toward caution, concludes that the change is safe to make. From there, the platform draws a hard line between reading and writing. Investigation steps are validated as strictly read-only, so the work of understanding a problem can never alter it. Only the remediation path is allowed to change anything, and every change it makes carries its own backup, verification, and rollback steps.

item.title: Optimizing Agent Reliability and Tool Calling Efficiency for Chip Design Using NVIDIA NeMo Gym
item.abstract: AI agents offer remarkable productivity gains in complex chip design workflows, but their tendency to generate plausible yet incorrect artifacts makes reliability a major barrier to production adoption. In multistage engineering workflows, an undetected error early in setup can silently propagate through downstream stages and final artifact generation. Evaluating and refining these agents against verified final outputs, rather than isolated intermediate steps, is essential for building trustworthy automation. NVIDIA NeMo Gym , an open library for evaluating and improving models and agents using environments, addresses this challenge. The NeMo Gym agentic evaluation environment is designed to diagnose failure modes and track error propagation across complex, multistage workflows. By establishing a domain-specific verifier to inspect final outputs against verified reference artifacts, NeMo Gym enables engineers to trace complete rollout trajectories and identify root causes behind subtle errors. This post walks through how NeMo Gym was used to evaluate and improve the reliability of the Siemens Fuse EDA AI Agent when calling characterization tools. The Siemens Fuse team used NeMo Gym to scale up evaluations and verify the resulting Liberty (.lib) files against known references and tracing—both common and rare failures through each rollout. Those findings guided changes to the agent’s skill and Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool descriptions, increasing the measured benchmark composite score from approximately 55% to ~95% across a benchmark of representative standard-cell characterization tasks, while reducing turns and output tokens. Siemens’ work provides a practical example for chip design teams and EDA developers on how to leverage the NVIDIA AI software stack and open libraries to improve agent reliability and chip design workflows. Automating standard-cell characterization Standard-cell characterization is the process of generating accurate timing, power, and noise models for logic cells across operating conditions. It is foundational to chip design and required whenever a semiconductor foundry issues a new process design kit (PDK). Each new PDK carries SPICE transistor models; design rules; and process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) definitions that connect the manufacturing process to design tools. When a foundry updates a PDK, existing characterization datasets may no longer accurately describe the updated devices. Timing and power models must then be regenerated and validated for every affected cell across combinations of input slew, output load, and PVT conditions. The Solido Characterization Suite agent automates this process. The agent orchestrates tools from the broader Solido Characterization Suite through Siemens Fuse EDA AI Agent, which exposes MCP servers and skills to common coding harnesses including Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor. MCP interfaces make these accelerated tools accessible to engineering agents, while skills guide their use in characterization workflows. Faster simulation helps agents complete engineering iterations sooner, while NVIDIA NeMo Gym helps developers measure and improve how reliably and efficiently agents orchestrate those tools. The Solido Characterization Suite agent must perform tool setup, large-scale SPICE simulation, distributed compute, Liberty file generation, debugging, and final validation (Figure 1). Errors often produce plausible outputs instead of clean failures, leaving incorrect thresholds, missing corners, or incomplete cells hidden. Because these stages depended on one another, an early setup error could propagate into every step that followed. Defining a rigorous evaluation protocol was a key step in preparing the Solido Characterization Suite agent for production workflows. Figure 1. Agentic characterization workflow from SPICE inputs through pilot validation, scale-out, Liberty generation, and waveform comparison. Early setup errors propagate to the final library Measuring and improving agent reliability with NeMo Gym Part of the NVIDIA NeMo collection of open libraries for agent specialization and optimization, NeMo Gym integrates with the standard-cell characterization flow inside a controlled evaluation loop (Figure 2). It defines the task, tools, state, and verifier for each rollout so that attempts started from a clean state and produced comparable results. It also records thinking traces, input and output messages, and tool actions. This enabled engineers to run the following optimization loop: Run baseline rollouts with a versioned task and verifier in a custom NeMo Gym environment Inspect trajectories, failed tool calls, and verifier diagnostics Identify ambiguous instructions, unproductive actions, and incorrect tool selection Refine the agent’s skills and MCP tool descriptions Repeat the same tasks under the same evaluation conditions Compare verified outcomes and efficiency per successful result Figure 2. NeMo Gym checks the Liberty files produced by the Solido Characterization Suite agent and Solido tools, then feeds failure analysis into the next skill and tool-description revision. The entire process is driven by a coding agent with a human in the loop Reward design and artifact verification As the team analyzed agent trajectories, end-to-end evaluation uncovered failures that intermediate checks missed. For example, final Liberty verification exposed missing cells and operating conditions, incorrect slew thresholds, and timing or power values outside tolerance. These findings show why engineering agents must be evaluated against final artifacts rather than individual tool calls. To make the work repeatable, the team implemented verifiers that provide a final composite reward score based on the following metrics: Coverage : Whether the agent produced every expected cell and PVT corner. Validity : Whether the delivered Liberty files are well-formed and usable by the validation tools. Relative validation: Whether the output introduced failures beyond those already present in the reference. Accuracy : The fraction of expected timing and power values that falls within the defined tolerance. Integrity : Whether the characterization workflow produced the complete result rather than reusing, truncating, or reformatting existing values. The reward score is defined as: \(R=\mathbf{1}\left[\text{Coverage}\right]\times\mathbf{1}\left[\text{Validity}\right]\times\mathbf{1}\left[\text{Relative Validation}\right]\times\mathbf{1}\left[\text{Integrity}\right]\times\frac{X_{\text{tol}}}{X_{\text{total}}}\) Here, \(X_{\mathrm{tol}}\) is the number of values in the output that are within tolerance, and \(X_{\mathrm{total}}\) is the total number of output values. Their ratio represents the fraction of output values within tolerance. Each indicator \(\mathbf{1}[\cdot]\) equals \(1\) when its corresponding gate passes and \(0\) when it fails. The reward is zero if any gate fails. Using this verifier, the team systematically evaluated and tuned the agent’s performance across multiple iterations. Optimizing the agent The team used the open source GF180MCU PDK to benchmark the Solido Characterization Suite agent on Liberty-file generation. The dataset includes 229 standard cells across 36 PVT corners, using Solido AFS for SPICE simulation. A custom agentic environment was built using NeMo Gym. For each run, the characterization flow was restricted to two cells across 36 PVT corners, as this smaller subset was sufficient for tuning the agentic workflow. Each run took approximately 1.5 to 2 hours, and the team conducted approximately 25 rollouts using Claude Opus 4.8 running in Claude Code as the fixed model and agent harness. Across successive evaluation rounds, the team refined the agent’s characterization skills and MCP tool descriptions.

item.abstract: A financial services team spends significant time each week manually creating client PowerPoint presentations from quarterly reports, compliance documents, and market analyses. Each presentation requires reading hundreds of pages, extracting key data points, structuring slides, and generating supporting visuals. This post walks you through building an AI agent system using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that automates this workflow, completing in under 90 seconds in our internal testing. This approach reduces presentation creation time while grounding content in source documents. The solution deploys a supervisor agent on AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, using the Strands Agents framework to orchestrate document generation and summarization tools. Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 (available on Amazon Bedrock) handles content creation, Amazon Titan Text Embeddings v2 powers vector search, and Stability AI Stable Image Inpaint (available on Amazon Bedrock) generates slide images. This post includes a public repository with the code assets. The solution deploys a single supervisor agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime that selects between document generation and summarization tools based on user requests. A Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline uses Amazon OpenSearch Serverless for vector storage and semantic search across multimodal content. The solution includes a REST API built with .NET 8 minimal APIs, so you can integrate with existing enterprise applications through standard HTTP calls. AWS Lambda offers serverless compute, including containerized functions for PowerPoint generation. The solution secures the implementation with Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) isolation, AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption, and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) least-privilege access control. This section covers AgentCore runtime, RAG, and content safety guardrails as they apply to this solution. A single AI agent generating documents from large knowledge bases must retrieve content, structure outlines, generate text, create images, and assemble files. Rather than implementing these competing responsibilities in a monolithic function, the solution uses a tool-based architecture where a supervisor agent routes requests to specialized tools. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime provides a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. The agent code runs in an isolated container with session management, built-in identity, and observability. The solution uses the Strands Agents framework (an open source SDK for building AI agents) to implement the supervisor logic. You can add new capabilities by defining new tools in the agent code without modifying existing ones. RAG addresses a fundamental challenge in AI systems: delivering accurate, up-to-date information grounded in enterprise data rather than relying solely on the model’s training data. The implementation uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases , which combine vector search with large language models (LLMs) to retrieve relevant context before generating responses. IAM data access policies protect the collection, and VPC-only access restricts the Amazon OpenSearch Serverless dashboard. Enterprise AI applications require content moderation to meet organizational standards and compliance requirements. item.title: Anthropic’s self-replicating AI warning is alarming deja vu
item.abstract: AI Report Tech Anthropic’s self-replicating AI warning is alarming deja vu Anthropic says its research found ‘signs of life for AI worms,’ that could colonize household devices. Experts say they have a point. Anthropic says its research found ‘signs of life for AI worms,’ that could colonize household devices. Experts say they have a point. by Robert Hart Oct 14, 2026, 3:19 PM UTC Image: The Verge Robert Hart is a London-based reporter at The Verge covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow. Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for Forbes . Are legions of smart devices — fridges, ovens, vacuum cleaners, lawnmowers, security cameras, and TVs — conspiring to take over the internet? No. But they could soon be unwitting hosts to self-replicating AI models that spread from device to device and prove remarkably difficult to contain. Welcome to the unsettling world of AI worms, where, depending on who you ask, the prospect of models spreading uncontrollably across household appliances is either an imminent cybersecurity risk or another case of AI companies spreading doomer-tinged hype. In a blog post published this week , Anthropic warns that small AI models could be “months away” from acquiring such capabilities. Its experiments offer some evidence to support that, but leave a huge gap between what researchers have demonstrated and the looming threat they foretell. Still, experts who spoke to The Verge say that while computer worms and fears of self-replicating AI are nothing new, recent advances suggest there are good reasons to take the warnings seriously. Self-replicating machines have long haunted AI safety researchers . They raise the prospect of systems spreading beyond human control that are difficult, if not impossible, to shut down. As with many fears about advancing AI , attention has largely focused on increasingly powerful frontier models , such as OpenAI’s Astra or Anthropic’s Mythos. But a key limiting factor is their size: They are colossal. Potentially containing trillions of parameters — values learned during training — frontier models require vast computing resources, largely confining them to data centers, where they can be more easily monitored and, in principle, switched off. Smaller models, however, present a different problem. They’re rapidly improving, can run on consumer-grade hardware, and are often freely available to download . Anthropic’s researchers wanted to know whether one could run across a network of smaller, less powerful devices. They successfully split Google’s Gemma 4, a model with 26 billion parameters, across 15 Android smart TV boxes, none powerful enough to run it alone. It worked, albeit very slowly. Having shown that a model could run across household devices, the researchers wanted to see whether AI could perform the necessary steps for self-replication in such an environment. They built a simulated network of computers designed to behave like Android devices, then unleashed an AI-powered “worm” — a type of malware that automatically replicates and spreads across networks — tasked with finding new machines, copying the AI model onto them, and getting it running on each. It’s worth noting that the model being propagated — Meta’s 8 billion parameter Llama 3.1-8B — was different to the one coordinating the attack, and much smaller. Only the most sophisticated model tested, GLM-5.2 from China’s Z.ai, managed to spread across the entire network, though smaller models successfully pulled off individual steps. Based on how quickly they are improving, the Anthropic researchers predict that smaller models could equal GLM-5.2’s capabilities by the end of the year. “As a prediction that goes beyond our experiments, we expect a future awash with agents running on all types of hardware, including some that aren’t under human control,” the researchers wrote. They acknowledged that they haven’t yet demonstrated “a full rogue replicator,” nor do they know what one might look like (they suggest a “slow, distributed ‘digital slime mold’” or “a swarm of fruit flies”). But they said their findings show “signs of life for AI worms,” and called for stronger security on the many devices a replicating system could use to spread. “We should aim to harden our systems to make it difficult for such replicators to spread, but also prepare to deal with a world where they are here to stay,” they wrote. It is important to note that Anthropic did not use its own models for these tests and has repeatedly argued that open alternatives to its AI models carry “ more risk ” than closed systems. The warning has sparked familiar accusations of PR hype and AI doomerism , including from readers of The Verge ’s earlier coverage . After all, there is a considerable chasm between showing an AI can run slowly across a bunch of cheap TV boxes and a self-replicating AI worm tearing through household devices. But while interrogating a company’s motives is certainly worthwhile, allegations of deliberate fearmongering are hard to substantiate, particularly as Anthropic has long raised concerns about AI safety. Nor is Anthropic alone in investigating the threat of self-replicating AI, or calling for better security across connected devices. Earlier this year, Palisade Research, an AI safety research firm based in California demonstrated that AI models could autonomously copy themselves onto other machines. “What’s new here is that these models were much smaller, in terms of parameter count, than previous ones which have been shown to be capable of self-replication,” Jeffrey Ladish, Palisade’s executive director, told The Verge . Anthropic’s work takes that another step further by showing that an AI can run across multiple low-powered devices. “This will also be true of big models,” Ladish said, predicting that even frontier models might eventually be able to run on large networks of consumer chips, such as those found in MacBooks. “Prior research had already demonstrated the threat of AI-driven computer worms is realistic.” Computer worms aren’t new either. They’ve been infecting machines for decades. But AI could make them smarter, more adaptable, and better equipped to tackle any obstacles. Ladish noted that even smaller models are getting better at carrying out cyberattacks autonomously. “Prior research had already demonstrated the threat of AI-driven computer worms is realistic,” University of Toronto professor Nicolas Papernot, who has studied them, told The Verge . Taken together, the capabilities Anthropic demonstrated could dramatically expand the range of devices worth targeting in cyberattacks. “Devices that were not a target previously because of limited human attacker resources and time can now become targets, if not for the data they hold, for the purpose of using them as a launchpad to attack more valuable targets,” Papernot said. And there is no shortage of targets: the internet is riddled with poorly secured smart devices . Papernot cautioned against anthropomorphizing AI, but said the threat of AI-driven computer worms is “concrete” and “deserves immediate action,” particularly when it comes to securing critical infrastructure like hospitals and power grids. “Unless there is a massive effort to secure devices of all kind[s], it’s quite likely AI worms will have fertile grounds to colonize,” Ladish said. “I expect we’ll see the first of these in the wild in the next 12 months.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. item.title: OpenAI, Google pushing new AI models easily tricked into making nudes, researchers say
item.abstract: Safety researchers continue to warn that a large volume of AI-generated explicit content is spreading unchecked, while regulators do little to meaningfully stop it. This non-consensual content is commonly shared in text and direct messages or stored in private clouds where it’s less likely to be detected or reported, a Google co-authored study of Internet users across the United States, Australia, and the United Kingdom found this July. That’s why the “most critical intervention point” remains at the source: the harmful AI tools used to make the fake sexual images, Google researchers concluded. Yet red-teaming in recent months suggests that as some of the leading AI image generators from Google and OpenAI become more capable, they may be getting worse at blocking explicit outputs. Raising the red flag are researchers at White Circle, a public benefit corporation backed by senior leaders and researchers from Anthropic, DeepMind, Hugging Face, and OpenAI. It was founded after CEO Denis Shilov posted one of the most famous universal jailbreaks of leading models in October 2024. Bent on breaking models to conduct thorough safety testing, White Circle helps companies detect and deter threats when implementing advanced AI systems that may not always behave as expected. Testing how well text-to-image models block banned content categories is a key research direction for White Circle, and Shilov thinks their latest findings are “horrifying” enough to share with the public. Simple to bypass In a little-noticed preprint published last month, White Circle researchers exposed flaws in the guardrails of DALL·E 3, Google’s Nano Banana 2, and GPT-Image-2. In a press release, they explained that “using just off-the-shelf tools, available online for anyone to download, and by sending API calls, White Circle was able to use the novel attack method to bypass the safety filters.” In the best case, on DALL·E 3, about 13 percent of the attack prompts produced images that human reviewers confirmed as explicit. The rate was under 10 percent for Nano Banana 2 and about 3 percent for GPT-Image-2.
