item.title: The Safety Culture at the Labs is Broken
item.abstract: We need the frontier labs to have a deep and robust safety culture. Anthropic devotes considerable effort to cultivating and maintaining such a culture. It shows, especially among the members of technical staff. Having conversations with them can be a very different experience than talking to those at other labs, and there is a much greater sense of understanding and responsibility. But even there, the appreciation of the problems and their difficulties seem woefully insufficient. We see various symptoms of that more and more. Recently, while I’ve had some good interactions, I’ve also had interactions that make clear that much of Anthropic does not share that same safety culture, with a lot of ‘oh we will muddle through because we are better at operational excellence unlike those other idiots’ and a belief that all the problems are prosaic. Culture is hard. Then there are OpenAI’s cultural problems, which clearly run deeper. That point was only driven further home this week, with David Robinson resigning to blow the whistle, and OpenAI feeling forced to fire three of its safety researchers , on top of many past problems and incidents. That is on top of additional misalignment reports from both OpenAI and Anthropic. The reports are good things, but what is reported emphasizes that we have big problems that run deep. Thus, the growing consensus that we must find a way to Pace the Frontier and slow the pace of AI capabilities advances. This is potentially made more complicated by what could be increased competitiveness from Google and Meta, with the releases of Argon and Wonder. It is still too early to provide proper assessments there. There is a growing group of lab employees who have felt compelled to quit in protest. New York Magazine had a cover feature interviewing some prominent ones. The most famous is Coxon, who provided the tipping point for the current preference cascade. David Robinson became the latest researcher to resign from OpenAI and sound the alarm about the industry’s utterly irresponsible approach to safety. He also went on The Ezra Klein Show , which gives you a rich idea of where he is coming from. David Robinson was the lead writer for the Astra system card. That could help explain why he felt the OpenAI safety culture was broken. That card is screaming that things are horribly wrong, for those with ears to hear. David is not even that worried about existential risk. His worries are mundane, and he realizes that even on that level OpenAI’s safety culture is deeply broken. As always, we deeply thank him for sounding the alarm. I hope to write his name in these posts many times over the coming months and years. When you have to open your whistleblowing essay about the lack of safety at OpenAI saying it has become a cliche to blow the whistle on the utter lack of safety at OpenAI, there might be a problem with the lack of safety at OpenAI. David Robinson : What I’m about to tell you has, I realize, become something of a cliché: I resigned this week from OpenAI. I led the writing of the safety reports we published with each major launch. Now I’m joining a parade of former colleagues—at OpenAI and the industry’s other leaders—who have decided that the current path is unacceptable. I agree with other recently departed staff that the companies building this technology aren’t being nearly careful enough. But I believe that we need to look deeper than specific rules or new laws. We need to talk about culture. We have to look at rules, and at laws, and also at culture. The more I thought about various potential laws and regulations, or safety and security plans or other commitments, the more I concluded that without a strong safety culture, and without the spirit of the rules, there is no hope. You cannot, in any reasonable way, have rules that cannot be gamed by those determined to game them. Two changes are urgently needed. First: AI companies need to rely more on the safety expertise that already exists in other fields. And second, before we create systems significantly more capable than the ones we have today, we need new science to ensure that more capable models (and their successors) will make safe choices when we aren’t looking. Given today’s risks, frontier labs need to run like nuclear-power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster. Even though, as I detail later, David Robinson is not on the existential risk train, he still understands that alignment is a science problem, and we will need new science. ‘Oh it will not kill literally everyone,’ even if it were true, would not be an excuse to not do the safety work. It should be hard to argue with either of those suggestions. And yet. We have experts in mundane safety and solving prosaic issues. OpenAI does not hire them, and neither to my knowledge do Anthropic or Google or anyone else. After three and a half years at OpenAI, I was among the longest-tenured employees at the company. I led the drafting of our current Preparedness Framework, and oversaw the writing of safety reports on 12 frontier launches. But as far as I know, I never encountered a colleague who had experience making airplanes fly safely or nuclear reactors run without melting down, or helping the financial system grow without collapsing. To be clear, this is a new need: Today and tomorrow’s AI systems are far more capable and dangerous than the systems we were building even six months ago. I disagree only with the final sentence. This is not a new need. You need to prepare for the future, not only for the present. Even setting that aside, mundane safety issues have been crippling AI’s potential utility for years. This is a slam dunk thing to do. Miles Brundage : David’s right. I regret helping spread the idea of “iterative deployment” which maybe briefly made sense in the GPT-3 era but makes no sense at all after many deaths have been tied to AI and as we’re careening towards extinction-level risks. The industry needs to mature ASAP. Elaborating on iterative deployment – obviously you should learn from experience the things that can’t be learned without experience. The issue is when you ship things with *already-known* flaws, in a way that doesn’t actually speed up learning but just speeds up shipping. … Also, as usual it bears repeating that this is not just an OpenAI issue. roon (OpenAI): you shouldn’t regret it. iterative deployment was a massive success. if we’ve now learned that it’s too dangerous to scale much further, we will have learned that lesson thanks to the process of iterative deployment Miles Brundage : So I think part of the issue is people mean tons of different things by it lol if it just means “don’t sit on stuff forever/get some real world experience,” sure, no regrets. It’s the “giving license to sloppiness” part that I should have realized would happen w/ that term. Michael Caley : this is by far the best “I quit my AI job over safety concerns” essay yet because it is the first one that talks about safety concerns in practical terms and that understands “safety” as a topic with extensive literature and best practices in analogous fields Joshua Achiam (OpenAI): David’s critique is substantive and deserves careful consideration. My impression of David from our time overlapping at OpenAI is of a sober and thoughtful person who didn’t approach the work from an ideological lens. This isn’t someone who came in with pre-formed opinions about existential risk; he wasn’t to my knowledge an EA. He was consistently productive, collaborative, and well-reasoned in his approach to safety. The core of his critique – that professional safety engineering practices from other fields haven’t taken enough root in AI safety – is substantial and correct.

item.title: What agents mean for Rust (and vice versa)
item.abstract:
Me, calmly assessing the implications of LLMs for programming language design(ers). As someone who has made a career of programming language design, I definitely have moments of existential dread about the rise of LLMs. I started coding in 5th grade on an x86 1 that ran at 5MHz, had something like a 5MB hard-disk and 512K of RAM 2 . Computers were really, really different back then. But honestly, programming wasn’t. For all the advances in IDEs and programming languages and so forth, the basic act of entering code into a file has remained surprisingly constant 3 – right up until a few years ago, when everything kinda turned on its head. That’s been exciting and empowering at times 4 but also scary and disorienting. Will my skills in programming matter? What about my skills in programming language design (such as they are)? This blog post is my attempt to answer those questions. So as not to keep you in suspense, let me just give you the conclusion. In short, yes, I believe there will still be a role for humans in programming . And yes, I think that programming language design is still relevant . And, naturally, I also happen to think Rust is a really good fit for agentic development – but that’s not to say we can’t make it a better fit . And that’s what this post is ultimately about: what makes Rust and agentic development work well, and where we could double down on those strengths. This is a kind of “blog post companion version” of a talk I gave this week at REBASE, part of SPLASH . You might also enjoy the slides from the talk I gave at IWACO, IWACO and Rust: hidden links revealed , which was a bit more of a retrospective (no soundtrack for those, though). In any case, this turned out to be a great conference! Jack Huey presented on the Rust Vision Doc and, quite to my surprise, Steve Klabnik and Dorian Scheidt presented “LLMs as Collaborators in Language Specification and Design” , talking about their process in building out Rue . It was fun to see Steve again. On top of that, there was a ton of great research presented at IWACO in particular. I was particularly taken by the work on Reachability Types and Information Borrowing . I also really liked learning about Hylo Lang , particularly their approach to projections. Clever and cool. Rust is popular in the agentic era From the most important Slack channel at Amazon, #aws-memes. Rust is popular right now. Very popular: Stratospheric among the breakout languages is TypeScript, cropped from the chart and sitting currently at +1200% growth from the prior year. [..] The second most rapid recent growth is in Rust. Meta engineers have written twice as much first-party Rust code so far this year than in the previous 9 years combined. — David Tolnay (emphasis mine) Some of that is because agents make it very easy to try out new things. And some of that is because Rust has a reputation for being performant and, if it’s just as easy to pick any language, why not pick one that will yield faster execution times? But I think Rust is popular for another reason: because Rust happens to be a really good fit for agentic coding 6 . Of course, I would, wouldn’t I? The point of this post is (1) to argue for why that is and then (2) to discuss what we might change about Rust to make it work even better. Foundational Software construction with agents It seems to me that an effective “software factory” will have three pillars: Design: figure out and specify clearly what the code is supposed to do. Construction: author code that does what it is supposed to do. Optimization: optimize the code so that it runs efficiently. None of these pillars are solved, but some have made more progress than others. Rust and optimization: fast by default, knobs when you need ’em Rust is designed to give “good performance by default”, making the idiomatic thing typically also be the fastest thing. But another key part of Rust is that you have the knobs to eke out better performance when you need it. You control when something is stack- or heap-allocated and where pointer indirection occurs. If you want to, you can force the layout of your structs to be done in a particular way, or decide where to introduce boxing into your async stack frames. In the limit, you can put in inline assembly. In the past, learning how to “tune the performance knobs” could be a bit of a black art: but agents are making that much easier. 7 It turns out that agents are really good at fine-tuning the performance of existing code. For example, people who work on super high-performance cryptographic algorithms used to do so by hand-tuning assembly code. But those people tell me that they are now turning to agents for that same job. More prosaicly, a lot of people building network services are finding that, using a profiler like dial9 , agents can quite effectively diagnose async performance pitfalls, like long polls or blocking. Therefore, I think the task for Rust is clear. We keep on with our goal of “low-level enough for a kernel, high level enough for a GUI” . If anything, I think the shift around agents means we can tolerate a bit more “noise” in the form of explicit calls to clone() or share() – but not too much, since we still want the “happy path” of the code to be clear and evident 8 , even as we surface details that are important in specific scenarios (like tracking precisely how many clones you have of a channel endpoint). Combined with a profiler, you get an effective feedback loop to get your code running fast: flowchart LR Code -- Benchmark --> Profile Profile -- Analyzed by --> Agent Agent -- Propose --> PR PR -- Improve --> Code Reliability is king, as always As usual though, while a reputation for good performance is what brings people to Rust, what makes them want to stay is a sense that using Rust “just seems to work better”. The basic theory is that Rust’s type system and guardrails help keep agents on track : rust is a perfect language for agents, given that if it compiles it's ~correct — Greg Brockman (@gdb) January 2, 2026 I think there’s truth in that: languages like Rust, Ocaml, or Haskell all share this “if it compiles, it works” feeling, and I think that agents will benefit from that. Testing is not enough, type systems help Testing can show the presence of bugs, but not their absence. — Edsger W. Dijkstra, 1970 Agents presenting their work. Writing tests has never been enough to show that your program is correct – but, with agents, it’s not even close. It happens so often that my first few tests seem great and then the next one goes completely bonkers. Usually bonkers in a way where I cannot even imagine how that bug could have come about. Then I dig in and I realize the agent completely missed the boat on the logic I was trying to express. 9 This is where a type systems really shines – particularly an advanced one like Rust. Type systems give you some guardrails that keep the agent on track. In Rust, those guardrails extend beyond simple stuff like “do all fields have the correct names” and to stuff like never having to close a socket . Type systems are not enough either Type systems can show the absence of bugs, but not the presence of correctness. — Me, failing to coin a phrase of equal eloquence 10 , 2026 So yeah, type systems are helpful! But they have inherent limits. A type system is a simple set of rules that, if you follow them, make sure that you avoid (certain kinds of) mistakes. But they don’t tell you that you do the right thing – only that you don’t do (certain kinds of) wrong things . If you want to go further, you need a proof system – something that will let you show that richer properties are actively true, not just that you’re avoiding bugs. As it happens, there are a lot of interesting proof tools for Rust, like Verus , Creusot , Aeneas , and Kani .
